lead: The ultimate load method (ULM), also called ultimate strength design or the load factor method, designs a section for collapse instead of for service stresses. The service loads are multiplied by a load factor to get the ultimate loads, and the section is made strong enough to carry them when its concrete and steel have reached their real, inelastic strengths. It came after the working stress method because tests showed that elastic stresses say little about the load at which a beam actually fails. Today it survives as the collapse half of limit state design.
prereq: You need: the working stress method and the stress–strain curves in properties of concrete and reinforcing steel.

blocks.text: Service loads are the loads expected in normal use: dead load wD from the member, finishes and walls, and live load wL from people, furniture and stored goods. A load factor γf is the number by which a service load is multiplied to get the ultimate load at which collapse is checked:

blocks.where: w<sub>u</sub> is the ultimate load per metre, γ<sub>f</sub> the load factor (for example 1.5), and w<sub>D</sub>, w<sub>L</sub> the service dead and live loads per metre, all in kN/m.

blocks.text: Different factors can be put on dead and live load, because live load is less certain, but the idea is the same: the whole margin of safety sits on the load side. The required ultimate moment follows from ordinary analysis: for a linear analysis M<sub>u,req</sub> = γ<sub>f</sub> M<sub>service</sub>, where M<sub>service</sub> is the moment from the service loads.

The ultimate moment of resistance Mu is the largest moment the section can carry before it fails. It is found from the real behaviour at failure: the concrete compression zone has the curved stress distribution of the stress–strain curve, and the tension steel has yielded and carries fy. No material factor is used; the materials enter at their characteristic strengths.

For a rectangular section use the idealised concrete curve without the material factor: a parabola to a strain of 0.002 and a flat top at 0.67fck to 0.0035. Its average stress over the compression depth xu is 0.67 × 17/21 = 0.542fck, and its resultant acts at 0.416xu below the top (the same shape as the limit state stress block, where the derivation is shown). Equilibrium gives
0.542 f<sub>ck</sub> b x<sub>u</sub> = f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>st</sub>,   M<sub>u</sub> = f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>st</sub> (d − 0.416 x<sub>u</sub>)
blocks.where: b is the width and d the effective depth in mm, A<sub>st</sub> the tension steel area in mm², x<sub>u</sub> the depth of the neutral axis at failure in mm.

blocks.text: The section is safe when M<sub>u</sub> ≥ M<sub>u,req</sub>. The ratio M<sub>u</sub>/Mservice is the real factor of safety against collapse, which WSM never computes.

sections.h3: Merits, drawbacks and why limit state design replaced it

items: Merit: it designs for the actual failure condition and uses the reserve of strength beyond the elastic range, so sections are smaller and cheaper than by WSM.
Merit: the load factor is a direct, understandable margin against collapse, and it treats dead and live load as loads, not as stresses.
Drawback: nothing in the method checks service behaviour. Slender sections made with high-strength steel can pass the collapse check and still deflect and crack badly under everyday load.
Drawback: one factor on the load cannot separate the scatter of concrete strength from that of steel strength.
Drawback: an over-reinforced section can fail suddenly by crushing; the method needs extra rules to keep failures ductile.

blocks.text: Limit state design kept the collapse check of ULM, split the single factor into partial safety factors on loads and on each material, and added explicit serviceability checks for deflection and cracking. IS 456 adopted the limit state method in its 1978 revision, and the 2000 edition retains it as the main method; see limit state philosophy and partial safety factors.

examples.question: A simply supported beam of span 6.0 m carries a service dead load of 12 kN/m and a service live load of 8 kN/m. Using the ultimate load method with a load factor of 1.5 on the total load, find the service moment and the required ultimate moment M<sub>u,req</sub>.
steps: Total service load w = w<sub>D</sub> + w<sub>L</sub> = 12 + 8 = 20 kN/m.
Service moment M<sub>service</sub> = w L²/8 = 20 × 6.0²/8 = 90 kNm.
Required ultimate moment M<sub>u,req</sub> = w<sub>u</sub> L²/8 = 30 × 36/8 = 135 kNm, which is 1.5 × 90.

examples.question: The beam of the first worked example is 300 mm wide with an effective depth of 500 mm and has 4 bars of 20 mm Fe415 as tension steel; the concrete is M20. Find its ultimate moment of resistance M<sub>u</sub> by the ultimate load method (no material factors), check it against M<sub>u,req</sub> = 135 kNm, and find the real factor of safety against collapse.
steps: A<sub>st</sub> = 4 × 314.2 = 1257 mm². Steel force at failure T = f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>st</sub> = 415 × 1257 = 521,500 N.
Check that the steel has yielded: steel strain = 0.0035 × (500 − 160.3)/160.3 = 0.0074, more than the yield strain 415/200,000 = 0.0021. The section is under-reinforced and fails in a ductile way.
Check: M<sub>u</sub> = 226 kNm ≥ M<sub>u,req</sub> = 135 kNm, so the section is safe at collapse.
Factor of safety against collapse = M<sub>u</sub>/Mservice = 226/90 = 2.5.
examples.answer: M<sub>u</sub> = 226 kNm ≥ 135 kNm, so the beam passes; it would collapse at about 2.5 times its service load. ULM says nothing about its deflection at 90 kNm.

traps: M<sub>u</sub> (the capacity of the section) and M<sub>u,req</sub> (the demand from ultimate loads) are different numbers; the check is M<sub>u</sub> ≥ M<sub>u,req</sub>. Writing M<sub>u</sub> = 135 kNm for the demand hides which side is which.

Apply the load factor once, to the loads. In ULM the materials enter at f<sub>ck</sub> and f<sub>y</sub> with no material factor; dividing by 1.5 and 1.15 as well turns it into limit state design and double-counts safety.
The concrete stress at failure is not f<sub>ck</sub>: the flat top of the curve is 0.67f<sub>ck</sub>, because concrete in a member is weaker than a test cube.
Passing the ULM check does not prove the beam serviceable; the method has no deflection or crack check.
Keep units: w in kN/m and L in m give M in kNm; forgetting the square on L gives a moment six times too small for a 6 m span.

quiz.a: The number by which a service load is multiplied to obtain the ultimate load at which collapse is checked.

quiz.q: State the collapse check of the ultimate load method.
quiz.a: M<sub>u</sub> ≥ M<sub>u,req</sub>: the ultimate moment of resistance of the section must be at least the moment caused by the ultimate (factored) loads.

quiz.q: Why can a beam designed by ULM be unsatisfactory in service?
quiz.a: ULM checks only collapse. A slender section with high-strength steel can carry the ultimate load and still deflect and crack excessively at service load, which nothing in the method checks.

quiz.q: What is the difference between ultimate load and ultimate strength?
quiz.a: Ultimate load is the factored load acting on the member (the demand). Ultimate strength is the capacity of the section at failure (the resistance).

quiz.q: A 5 m simply supported beam carries 10 kN/m dead and 6 kN/m live load at service. With a load factor of 1.5, find M<sub>u,req</sub>.
quiz.a: w = 16 kN/m; w<sub>u</sub> = 24 kN/m; M<sub>u,req</sub> = 24 × 5²/8 = 75 kNm.

quiz.q: A section has M<sub>u</sub> = 150 kNm. With a load factor of 1.5, what is the largest service moment it may carry?
Why does the same beam show a factor of safety of 2.5 by ULM when the load factor was only 1.5?
quiz.a: The beam was given more steel than the minimum needed: its M<sub>u</sub> of 226 kNm exceeds M<sub>u,req</sub> of 135 kNm by a ratio of 1.67, and 1.5 × 1.67 = 2.5. The load factor is the minimum margin required, not the margin the chosen section has.

quiz.q: Which weaknesses of ULM led to limit state design?
quiz.a: No serviceability checks, and one factor that lumps load and material uncertainty together. Limit state design adds deflection and crack checks and separate partial safety factors on loads and on concrete and steel.

beyond: Collapse analysis has moved well past a single section: plastic hinge analysis of frames, yield line analysis of slabs and nonlinear finite element models now predict the collapse load of whole structures, and load rating of old bridges uses the same idea. Full-scale tests still calibrate these methods. Search next for "plastic analysis of RC frames", "yield line theory" and "nonlinear analysis of reinforced concrete".
